Molecular mechanism: Two dCas9 orthologs carry complementary leucine zippers; post-translational heterodimerization bridges the two bound sites
Components to deliver / co-express: 2 proteins: SpdCas9–Zip, StdCas9–Zip • 2 sgRNAs (4 to multiplex)
Multiplexing demonstrated: Yes — 4 sgRNAs give 4 single or 2 double loops at one reporter
Genomic scale: Loops 1.4–4.7 kb • enhancer–promoter contact across 11.7 kb
Readout / structural evidence: 3C (1.7 kb only) • LacI loop-assistance β-gal assay • qRT-PCR
Reported performance: ~15–17% looping at 4.7 kb; ~40% at 1.4 kb • 4 sgRNAs raised LacI looping ~1.7-fold, to ~58% • ~3-fold reporter activation across 11.7 kb • ~2-fold on endogenous norVW
Advantages: Fully encoded, no inducer • first quantitative model of engineered looping • strength tunable by guide number
Key limitations: Bacteria only • weak DNA binding (KDNA ≈ 105 nM) is rate-limiting • over-expression breaks loops • the norVW enhancer was inserted, not native • static, no temporal control

Molecular mechanism: Two spacers joined by an RNA linker in one transcript recruit two dCas9; the RNA itself bridges the sites, with no protein dimerization interface
Inducible (trigger): No — induction acts on dCas9 expression, not loop assembly
Genomic scale: In vivo up to >4.5 kb • in vitro 160 bp–2.4 kb
Readout / structural evidence: AFM and TEM (direct loop imaging, in vitro) • β-galactosidase assay (in vivo) • 3C attempted and failed
Reported performance: AFM loop yield ~50% at 160 bp, 12% at 2.1 kb • TEM inter-dCas9 spacing ~100 Å, linker-independent • repression sustained 6–8 h • in vivo repression not quantified in the text
Advantages: Minimal architecture — one protein, one RNA • the best fit among looping tools for size-constrained vectors
Key limitations: Bacteria only • in vivo loop inferred from repression alone • repression not determined by inter-site distance • no reversibility, multiplexing or eukaryotic data

Molecular mechanism: Two dCas9 orthologs carry PYL1 and ABI1; abscisic acid drives their heterodimerization, juxtaposing the loci
Components to deliver / co-express: 2 proteins: SpdCas9–PYL1, SadCas9–ABI1 • 2 sgRNAs • abscisic acid
Inducible (trigger): Yes — abscisic acid • loop detectable at 24 h
Reversible: Yes after short induction; after 10 days the contact became washout-resistant in K562 but not in HEK293T
Target loci: HBB ↔ LCR HS2 • POU5F1 ↔ distal 5′ enhancer
Reported performance: Loop within 24 h • expression changes significant but not quantified as fold-changes • the same LCR–β-globin loop activated transcription in K562 but not in HEK293T
Advantages: First mammalian inducible and reversible looping platform • shows the transcriptional effect of an identical loop is cell-type dependent
Key limitations: Two orthogonal Cas systems plus a chemical inducer • reversibility lost after prolonged induction, cell-type dependent • no distance ceiling established • expression not quantified

Molecular mechanism: A dCas9–CIBN anchor occupies both sites; blue light drives CIBN–CRY2 dimerization and CRY2 oligomerization, clustering the loci
Components to deliver / co-express: 2 proteins: dCas9–CIBN, soluble CRY2 • 4 gRNAs (2 per anchor)
Inducible (trigger): Yes — blue light, 470 nm • loop after 4 h
Reversible: Not demonstrated — proposed only, with no washout or dark-recovery data
Multiplexing demonstrated: 4 gRNAs for a single loop • independent loops not shown
Genomic scale: ~540 kb — the largest engineered loop in the table
Reported performance: Loop strength +2.0–2.5-fold under light • only +1.2–1.3-fold Zfp462 expression • smFISH 53.5 vs 43.7 mRNA per cell
Advantages: Fastest and most precisely timed trigger • no chemical cofactor • clearest evidence that contact frequency and transcription are loosely coupled
Key limitations: Interaction strength modest in this first implementation • reversibility untested • one loop in one cell type • blue light constrains in vivo use

Molecular mechanism: sgRNAs carry adapter sequences that hybridize to synthetic clickable oligonucleotides; SPAAC or SPIEDAC ligation covalently bridges the loci
Components to deliver / co-express: 1 protein: dCas9 • 2 sgRNAs with adapter sequences • 2 ssCOA oligonucleotides
Fully genetically encodable: No — the ssCOA adaptors cannot be encoded
Inducible (trigger): Yes — adding ssCOAs • contacts within 6 h, persisting ≥10 days
Reversible: Yes — baseline 3 days after ssCOA withdrawal, or 1 day after light
Multiplexing demonstrated: Yes — two independent loops in one cell without cross-talk, plus a three-anchor hub
Reported performance: Ligation efficiency >80% in vivo • contacts induced at 6 h, persisting ≥10 days • POU5F1 activation highest with both chemistries; the hub exceeded a single loop • transcript induction not quantified
Advantages: The only system here to build multiple independent contacts in one cell • covalent rather than equilibrium linkage
Key limitations: Requires exogenous synthetic oligonucleotides • one cell line • 3C only, no genome-wide map • no off-target assay • transcription not quantified

Molecular mechanism: Targeted CpG methylation of a CTCF-binding site blocks CTCF anchoring and opens the insulated neighbourhood
Target loci: CBS at the miR290 and Pou5f1 loops
Genomic scale: Cross-boundary contacts to genes in the adjacent loop
Readout / structural evidence: 3C • CTCF ChIP • bisulfite sequencing • dCas9 ChIP-seq
Reported performance: CTCF binding significantly reduced, reported qualitatively • 3C showed increased contact between the enclosed super-enhancer and a gene in the neighbouring loop • the activated genes lie outside the targeted neighbourhood; genes inside were unaffected • 18 off-target sites, marginal methylation
Advantages: First evidence that topology can be reshaped by targeted epigenetic editing alone • matched dead-enzyme and scrambled-gRNA controls
Key limitations: No quantitative values for methylation, CTCF loss, contacts or expression • reversibility and heritability not assessed

Molecular mechanism: Repressive or methylating effectors displace CTCF from insulator motifs, weakening boundary insulation
Reversible: Effector-dependent: KRAB reverses on protein loss; DNMT3A3L methylation is heritable through mitosis
Target loci: PDGFRA boundary • OLIG2 • TAL1 • LMO2 • GIRK4
Multiplexing demonstrated: 10 CTCF sites assayed • KRAB reduced binding at 8 of 10
Readout / structural evidence: CTCF ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR • bisulfite sequencing • 4C-seq • RNA-seq
Reported performance: KRAB: −83% CTCF at P1, matching −81% by Cas9 editing; −95% in stable cells • DNMT3A methylated 20–40% of alleles, DNMT3A3L more • ~20% methylation retained 12 days after expression ceased • reduced promoter–insulator contact; PDGFRA upregulated
Advantages: Establishes the design rule that only gRNAs on the CTCF motif itself displace CTCF • epigenetic displacement matches DNA cleavage without cutting
Key limitations: Outcomes are strongly context-dependent • contacts and expression reported qualitatively • no off-target analysis for the combination

System / construct: dCas9 as a steric competitor at CBSs
Molecular mechanism: dCas9 bound at a CTCF site occludes CTCF; tested in vitro as a physical obstacle to cohesin translocation
Reversible: In principle — occupancy, not a covalent mark
Model system: Single-molecule assay with human cohesin and NIPBL–MAU2
Target loci: DNA substrates carrying CTCF and dCas9 sites
Readout / structural evidence: Single-molecule imaging of individual CTCF and cohesin — direct structural evidence
Reported performance: dCas9 blocked extrusion in only 5 ± 10% of encounters, despite being the larger protein • CTCF blocked 45 ± 9% from the N-terminal side, 16 ± 7% from the C-terminal side • tension-dependent: absent at zero force, 100% at ~0.14 pN
Advantages: Direct evidence that the CTCF barrier is a specific cohesin-binding function, not steric bulk
Key limitations: A negative result for tool design: dCas9 modulates CBS activity but does not substitute for CTCF boundaries • in vitro only; no in-cell occlusion efficiency

Molecular mechanism: A dCas9–CTCF fusion re-tethers CTCF to a promoter whose endogenous CTCF motif was deleted
Readout / structural evidence: PLAC-seq • in situ Hi-C • ChIP-seq • RNA-seq
Reported performance: Deleting the CTCF site reduced Vcan intra-TAD contacts, less severely than global CTCF loss • dCas9–CTCF restored those contacts and partially restored expression, with two distinct gRNAs • rescue required the partner promoter 350 kb away • fold-changes given only in the figures
Advantages: Shows that re-tethering CTCF rescues both architecture and transcription lost with an endogenous motif • the rescue depends on a defined distal partner
Key limitations: One locus, one cell system • no multiplexing • reversibility untested

Molecular mechanism: A truncated CTCF keeping the cohesin-interacting N terminus and two zinc fingers, but not the DNA-recognition module, is recruited by dCas9
Genomic scale: Target site >80 kb from the nearest endogenous CTCF site
Readout / structural evidence: ChIP-seq (CTCF, RAD21, SMC3) • C-TALE with virtual 4C • RNA-seq
Reported performance: N+2 produced a significant contact with the 3′-CBS and selective cohesin accumulation at the target • deleting the 5′-CBS upregulated HOXD3 305-fold, HOXD4 213-fold and HAGLR 24-fold • N+2 partially restored the lost contacts
Advantages: Shows extrusion-control modules can be separated from DNA recognition • avoids the off-target binding and cytotoxicity of full-length CTCF fusions
Key limitations: Barrier activity inferred from cohesin accumulation, not directly shown • engineered contacts are weak • partial loop restoration did not reverse the epigenetic or transcriptional changes

Molecular mechanism: A SunTag array recruits multiple TET1 catalytic domains, demethylating methylation-sensitive CTCF sites in an imprinting control region
Reversible: Not by design — the intent is stable demethylation
Readout / structural evidence: Bisulfite and oxidative bisulfite sequencing • CTCF ChIP-qPCR • RT-qPCR
Reported performance: 5mC reduced 66–90% at day 3, still 76% demethylated at day 27 • CTCF occupancy +1.6 to +3.6-fold at day 6, still +2.4-fold at day 27 • H19 +1.8-fold, stable • IGF2 −2-fold at day 3 but back to control by day 27
Advantages: Among the most durable epigenetic edits at an architectural element • CTCF occupancy measured directly
Key limitations: No allele-specific assay was performed • off-target demethylation at the H19 promoter (~32%) • the IGF2 effect is transient • one cell line • no chromatin-conformation data

Molecular mechanism: dCas9–TET1 demethylates the MECP2 promoter on the inactive X while dCpf1–CTCF tethers CTCF to two flanking anchors; the two systems are orthogonal by PAM
Inducible (trigger): Yes — doxycycline induces the dCpf1–CTCF arm
Reversible: Not by design; reactivation decays from ~50% to ~30% by day 20
Model system: Engineered hESC and derived cortical neurons
Target loci: MECP2 promoter DMR on Xi • two flanking CTCF anchors
Multiplexing demonstrated: Yes — two orthogonal Cas proteins, two effectors, three guides
Readout / structural evidence: Bisulfite sequencing • CTCF ChIP-seq • 4C-seq • RNA-seq • electrophysiology
Reported performance: dCas9–TET1 alone restored 18.7% of MeCP2 protein in 11.2% of neurons; adding dCpf1–CTCF gave 36.6% in 23.8%, with mRNA at 59% of wild type • CTCF at both anchors doubled • soma size restored from 73% to 99% of wild type • firing and synaptic currents fully rescued • dCpf1–CTCF alone had no effect
Advantages: The most advanced integration of architectural and epigenetic editing, with a functional rescue endpoint • insulation adds measurably to epigenome editing alone
Key limitations: Both editors are too large for a single AAV • applies only to female patients carrying a wild-type allele • reactivation decays in directly edited neurons • engineered lines, not patient cells • no animal data

Molecular mechanism: A bacterial cohesin–dockerin pair links dCas9 to an inner-nuclear-envelope protein, tethering loci to the nuclear periphery
Target loci: Acentric plasmid • SCO2, ABP1, SAC7, HXK1, IDI1
Multiplexing demonstrated: Not demonstrated — the one multi-gRNA test failed
Reported performance: Plasmid perinuclear localisation 44.5% → 62.6% • best locus HXK1 51.3% → 71.5% with a single gRNA • other four loci gained 15–18% • plasmid segregation 4.6% → 12.6%, against 77.5% for a centromeric control
Advantages: A single gRNA replaces the engineered binding-site arrays of earlier tethering systems • no chemical inducer • the only tethering platform shown in yeast
Key limitations: No gene-expression or functional readout was measured • not inducible; reversibility untested • multiplexing failed • plasmid rescue is partial

Molecular mechanism: Abscisic acid drives dimerization between dCas9 and a compartment anchor — emerin, coilin or PML — repositioning loci between subnuclear compartments
Components to deliver / co-express: 2 proteins: dCas9–ABI, PYL1–anchor • sgRNAs • abscisic acid
Inducible (trigger): Yes — abscisic acid • periphery 75% at 16 h, Cajal bodies 89% within 30 min
Reversible: Yes — periphery returns to baseline by 48 h, Cajal bodies within 24 h
Target loci: Chr3q29 • Chr13q34 • telomeres • XIST • PTEN • CXCR4
Multiplexing demonstrated: sgRNA pooling for one target • simultaneous repositioning to different compartments not shown
Genomic scale: Cajal-body repression measured 35 kb to 575 kb from the target
Reported performance: Periphery: Chr13 13% → 69%; PTEN 39% → 61% of loci and 62% → 88% of cells • Cajal bodies: Chr3 2% → 94%; PML bodies likewise 94% • repression of ACAP2 3.3-fold at 35 kb, PPP1R2 7.7-fold at 36 kb, TFRC 2.8-fold at 575 kb
Advantages: Three destination compartments from one architecture • inducible and reversible, with kinetics measured both ways • nucleates Cajal bodies de novo • works at a non-repetitive locus
Key limitations: Requires a chemical inducer • holding telomeres at the periphery cut viability by 72% over 6 days • peripheral repositioning is both mitosis-dependent and mitosis-independent

Molecular mechanism: Abscisic acid drives tiling of HP1α across a dCas9-targeted repeat array; HP1α dimerization and oligomerization build a compacting polymer
Components to deliver / co-express: 2 proteins: dCas9–ABI, PYL1–HP1α • 1 sgRNA per array • abscisic acid
Inducible (trigger): Yes — abscisic acid • 99.6% colocalisation within 1 h
Reversible: Yes, but slow and incomplete — 60% of puncta remain at 1.5 h after washout
Multiplexing demonstrated: Two arrays 200 kb apart on one chromosome • no two-chromosome test
Genomic scale: 29-kb array tiled • repression extends over 600 kb
Reported performance: Diffuse puncta 10.1% → 0.9% by 24 h • colocalisation of two arrays 200 kb apart 26% → 40% • repression reported only as moderate but significant, with no fold value • H3K9me3 unchanged
Advantages: The only tool that builds a heterochromatin polymer with its own disassembly kinetics
Key limitations: Requires high-copy tandem repeats; non-repetitive loci untested • the large fusion may impair some HP1α functions • one cell line • no fold repression reported • no chromatin-conformation assay

Molecular mechanism: A direct dCas9–emerin fusion drags sgRNA-bound DNA to the nuclear periphery, without any dimerizer
Inducible (trigger): Yes — sgRNA delivery • >80% of targets relocate within 3 min
Target loci: Plasmids and BACs • HSV-1 genomes • telomeres
Reported performance: >80% of episomes relocalised within 3 min, against a ~25% natural baseline • peripheral tethering reduced ICP27 mRNA 10-fold and inhibited virus production at all time points • telomeres repositioned far less efficiently, ~25% → ~38% at 3 h • virus titre reduction not quantified
Advantages: The fastest repositioning system reported • the only one establishing causality between subnuclear position and viral genome activity in both directions
Key limitations: No demonstrated reversibility • chromosomal repositioning much weaker than episomal • one cell line • virus-yield effects not quantified

Molecular mechanism: Light-induced recruitment of intrinsically disordered regions to a dCas9-targeted locus nucleates a local liquid condensate
Inducible (trigger): Yes — blue light • the rate of the light ramp sets targeting specificity
Reversible: Yes — the condensates are dynamic and reversible
Multiplexing demonstrated: One sgRNA seeds many repeat sites • droplets at distal sites fuse and pull loci together
Genomic scale: Reported in physical, not genomic units
Readout / structural evidence: Live-cell imaging • droplet and locus tracking • physical modelling
Reported performance: Droplets nucleate in low-density euchromatin and mechanically exclude non-targeted chromatin • coalescence generates forces estimated at 0.1–1 pN
Advantages: The only platform that moves chromatin by phase-separation forces rather than protein bridging, and quantifies them
Key limitations: No transcriptional measurement of any kind • forces are estimates, not measurements • repetitive loci only

Molecular mechanism: Chromatin-modulating peptides fused to Cas9 alter the local chromatin environment to improve access at nucleosome-occluded targets
Reported performance: Reported to improve activity up to several fold at refractory target sites, across seven Cas9 orthologs
Advantages: Portable across seven Cas9 orthologs, including compact ones • addresses how chromatin constrains CRISPR activity
Key limitations: Uses catalytically active Cas9 — an editing tool rather than an architecture tool
